title_en: The Star Wars Prequel Era Produced More Games Than You Can Shake a Lightsaber At – Here’s the Best, Worst, and Weirdest Ones
summary_en: There were more games released during Star Wars' prequel era than you can shake a lightsaber at, and while some of them were good, many were bad or really quite weird.
body_en:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer might be set in the New Republic era, but podracing screams “Star Wars Prequels” louder than Pepsi, and the bloodsport is largely beloved thanks to a video game.
The saga is no stranger to incredible games, but titles based on Episodes I, II, and III get lost easily among the KOTORs and TIE Fighters of the galaxy. The Prequel Trilogy has earned a second look from fans after Star Wars’ modern decade of disaster, and developers are starting to be at least Clone-curious with bangers like Zero Company .
The Prequels may have more motion than we thought, and it’s worth a trip back to BBY to explore their gaming past. Where can Star Wars games go from Galactic Racer onward, and what should be left behind like Anakin’s mom?
These are the best, worst, and weirdest Star Wars prequel trilogy games. We’ve got shooters, racers, and ecology simulators all on deck, so let’s start with the straight adaptations of the films:
The flagship game for Star Wars Episode I: The Phantom Menace released alongside the film in 1999. Like most Phantom Menace merch at the turn of the millennium, the game was a commercial success for PC and PlayStation, but that’s more indicative of the massive Star Wars Prequel hype than quality. They sold a lot of Jar Jar Binks lollipops too.
The game recreates the film from its opening tea service to the Battle of Naboo, controlling a veritable Mount Rushmore of beloved protagonists in Obi-Wan Kenobi, Qui-Gon Jinn, Padmé Amidala, and Captain Quarsh Panaka, all voiced by rather dubious soundalikes.
Fate is a big theme through the Prequel Trilogy, the idea that one’s destiny is fixed and uncontrollable. The same could be said of the camera in the Episode I game. Pinned high above your character, the POV renders gameplay extremely unpleasant as you leisurely lob blaster bolts back at battle droids. You can embrace the dark side and cut down innocent civilians who side-eye your rat-tail as you push boxes and complete fetch quests in a garish Otoh Gungah, but you won’t find it fun for long.
Jedi Power Battles is the superior game. Released a year later on PlayStation and Dreamcast, it follows Episode I’s entire plot in order, but only to the extent that Turtles in Time is invested in the story of Shredder stealing the Statue of Liberty. We’re in beat-’em-up territory, complete with a handful of fighters, combos and minigames, and a few fun secrets.
It’s far from the best example of the genre, but if you simply need to experience the plot of The Phantom Menace and you’ve had your fill of haggling and handmaiden intrigue, Power Battles is the answer.
There aren’t really many options for Episode II: Attack of the Clones. Scenes like the Geonisian arena and its kaizo platformer droid factory seemed tailor-made for games, but the starcrossed tale only received one proper adaptation: a ponderous sidescroller on the Game Boy Advance which fails to capture the burning passion of the film’s love story.
Episode III: Revenge of the Sith: the Movie : the Game fared much better. A hack-and-slash romp through 17 stages, it’s a bit like Power Battles with a bigger budget and some basic XP upgrades. It’s packed with unlockable characters and noncanonical missions where Anakin unalives everybody and seizes control of the galaxy. For a film that lives and dies by its duels, the single-player boss fights and PvP combat don’t miss. Even the ubiquitous handheld ports were solid.
The Episode III game oozes a prestige package. Cutscenes completely spoiled the film which came out ten days later, though there are some crucial differences for gameplay purposes that kind of make more sense than the movie, like Anakin personally killing Mace Windu to cement his Dark Side heel turn.
EA’s Lord of the Rings: Return of the King has a similar vibe, and also spoiled the heck out of its trilogy-topping movie before anyone could see it. The games are alike in a lot of ways, though from our point of view we’d give the edge to Mordor over Mustafar.
Whatever happened to games like these? It turns out you don’t need full-motion-video or fancy motion capture to convey the essence of a cinematic story. Sometimes all you need is a little Danish plastic.
Traveller’s Tales began their decades-long dominance of the licensed kid’s-game space with Lego Star Wars , whose simple title doesn’t need to stipulate that it’s covering the Prequel stories, because that’s just what “Star Wars” was in 2005.
The Prequel era appears in numerous Lego entries, largely delivered through grunts and pantomime without an ounce of gravitas, and it works. The first Lego Star Wars, with 6.1 million copies sold, is easily the most commercially successful Prequel Trilogy game despite largely being a joke.
Star Wars movies are vehicles for drama, action, and special effects. The plots and characters aren’t really built with controllers in mind, and the best Prequel games do well to explore their margins in side stories.
Some of the more interesting titles of the era are prequels to the capital “P” Prequels, like the Xbox-exclusive Star Wars: Obi-Wan . Not to be confused with the disappointing Disney+ show, or Obi-Wan’s Adventures, the Game Boy Color game that might be a better use of your time than the nine-figure streaming series.
Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan makes for a great protagonist. He literally sits out the worst parts of The Phantom Menace in a spaceship, so you don’t really associate him with extensive haggling and child slavery, and Jar Jar Binks and the Gungans do not appear at all in his self-titled game. Instead, we explore young Kenobi’s journey from the mean streets of Coruscant to the fateful Neimoidian breakout room that kicks off the entire saga.
Originally planned for PC, with a unique control scheme where mouse gestures controlled a lightsaber, the game was personally kiboshed by George Lucas and reworked for the launch window of Microsoft’s console. The padawan’s green blade, aglow with emerald Xbox synergy, would instead answer to the analog stick of the mighty Duke.
The exploits of Obi-Wan are nice to have, but Star Wars: Bounty Hunter has a lot more to explain. Released shortly after Attack of the Clones in 2002 and set years before Jango Fett’s decapitation, it tells the story of how the simple man making his way in the universe was chosen to stand at stud for an army of armored doppelgangers.
You’re given access to Jango’s entire arsenal and a surprising amount of freedom, blasting through seedy underbellies with a jetpack and roasting civilians and bounty targets alike. Industrial Light and Magic and Skywalker Sound all worked directly with LucasArts for the first time to create the game’s cutscenes, with great performances from the movies’ Temuera Morrison, plus Clancy Brown as a rival Mandalorian bounty hunter who is no longer compatible with canon.
The story explores the unsavory side of Star Wars, the dirty, dangerous places far from the Force where crime lords rule with a cortosis fist and a guy like Jango fits right in. Bounty Hunter was cited as an inspiration for the doomed “1313” project, and you don’t have to squint too hard to see shades of Andor, either.
Films convey character much differently than video games, a medium where Kyle Katarn and Cal Kestis carry more clout than Luke and Leia. Star Wars games are great at focusing on characters that the movies don’t have time for. The foxholes of a galactic war are filled with Iden Versios.
Begun in Episode II, the Clone Wars were, a brutal conflict that rages across 400 billion stars and largely takes place off screen. Wrapped up tidily in Episode III, the Clone Wars created a huge void that expanded media was well fit to fill.
Released in 2002 for PS2 and GameCube, “ Star Wars: The Clone Wars ” waged the opening salvos from behind the wheel. Developer Pandemic used the vehicular combat game as a testing ground for the in-house Zero engine that would usher in the era of Battlefront and its many Prequel Trilogy trappings.
A GBA game, New Droid Army , emerged around the same time, while the amusing Age of Empires reskin Galactic Battlegrounds rolled out a Clone Campaigns DLC that let you lead the fight against space tariffs by playing as the evil Separatists.
These titles barely scratched the limitless possibilities offered by a war fought over trade routes between clones and robots. An animated series or two was in order.
Genndy Tartakovsky's god-tier Clone Wars microseries made the fight look actually cool for the first time, but its only interactive representation came as a Flash-based browser game. Dave Filoni, the ascended fan who now essentially runs Lucasfilm, cut his teeth on his own Clone Wars series in 2008, and this one made the leap from Cartoon Network to consoles.
Republic Heroes is a bog-standard platformer, while Jedi Alliance takes advantage of the DS’s stylus swiping for its dual-character lightsaber skirmishes. Both games meet the standard of “whelming” one might expect from a spinoff to a spinoff, but they’re overshadowed by “ The Clone Wars: Lightsaber Duels ,” the game every single person imagined the first time they held a Wii Remote.
The plot takes a back seat to motion-control action, de-emphasizing the outsourced assassination and turgid love affair that defines the film. Instead, it zeroes in on one memorable aspect of the movies for a fun and satisfying power fantasy as a vertical slice of the saga.
Lore is great. Expanded Universes are beloved for a reason. There are thousands of well-worn paperbacks yellowing in the Legends library that can attest to that, but too much lore can elbow out the cinematic impact that made Star Wars a phenomenon. What is “Star Wars” if not a series of archetypical characters engaged in blockbuster setpieces, any one of which could be separated from the whole as a standalone experience?
The trench run, the Battle of Hoth, Teras Kasi kombat… You can carve out any given ten minutes from a Star Wars movie and probably find a decent game in there. “Spaceship combat” was the first place anyone looked, which quickly evolved into a sub-line of respectable flight sims and shooters.
1998’s Rogue Squadron was an Original Trilogy affair, but the devs at Factor 5 included a secret that evaded even GameShark detection for seven months. The UK release of The Phantom Menace was celebrated by revealing the Naboo Starfighter that was hidden in the code. A gleaming art deco Buck Rogers ship that mogged the busted-up Y-wings in the Rebel hangar, the Starfighter made it clear that the future was here, and it was all about the past.
Battle for Naboo is Rogue Squadron with a Prequel coat of paint. Like its predecessor, it’s a mission-based series of skirmishes that makes the most of the N64 Expansion Pak, with a propulsive plot powered by dialogue and dogfights.
The Starfighter itself is back, with a little less aura now that we’ve seen a nine-year-old boy master it in seconds, along with a fleet of the finest ships the Royal Security Forces have to offer. Unlike other games in the series, you play as RSF Lieutenant Gavyn Sykes throughout the whole story. Cool guy, but he’s no Wedge Antilles.
Battle for Naboo is exactly what you’d expect from Rogue Squadron: the Episode I version. The game is most notable for including concept art and an hour of developer’s audio commentary crammed into the N64 cartridge. It was especially impressive in 2001, when DVDs spoiled us with treats and bonus features. We at IGN were sure it was going to be the beginning of a major development trend to come. You can’t always get it right for 30 years.
Factor 5 took their talents back to the OT for the GameCube’s twin Rogue Squadrons, but LucasArts didn’t leave the Prequel age behind.
2001’s Starfighter , the series PS2 debut, is no slouch. Less Star Fox than Ace Combat, the game mixes sim and arcade as it weaves through the narrative of Episode I from the perspective of three characters, including fan favorite Nym, a mononomic space pirate who would one day earn an 18,000 word Wookiepedia article.
Nym and his signature ship, Havoc, would return the next year in Jedi Starfighter , scrapping with Separatists in the antebellum of the Clone Wars. It’s a fuller package than its predecessor, but both rate highly among Prequel games.
For all its faults, the Prequel Trilogy always excelled when it came to space and aerial action, full of big battles between cool looking ships that sound awesome. Now this is podracing!
Actually, this is podracing: Thanks to George Lucas’s lifelong fascination with fast cars, so much of Star Wars is propelled by the energy of a showstopping death race, a promise fully realized in the Phantom Menace.
The film’s entire second act revolves around the Boonta Eve Classic, a 500 mile-an-hour grand prix through the twisted canyons of Tatooine. For the competitors, ILM dreamed up enough pilots to fill a Glup Shitto graveyard, most of whom die horribly while Greg Proops cracks wise. Star Wars: Episode I Racer dares to ask: What’s their story?
The 1999 game for N64 and PC features 23 playable pods, nearly all doomed to expire on Boonta Eve.
We embody racer Ratts Tyerell, family man, racking up wins and wupiupi in the months before he’s vaporized. We become Ben Quadinaros as he purchases pit droids and upgrades his extremely dangerous ride so it doesn’t fail when he needs it most. We are Anakin, forced against our will to endure Watto’s gurgling as we dream of freedom on the track.
There’s little combat in the game for technical reasons, and while it diminishes the chariot race tension of the movie, it’s still a standout racer on a system that had a lot of them.
A code allowed you to dual wield two N64 controllers, analog sticks akimbo as you cranked the engines yanking you toward victory or oblivion. It almost felt like the real thing. The arcade game basically was the real thing.
SEGA created several Star Wars cabinets with interesting hardware, but nothing ever let you enter the world of Star Wars butt-first like Star Wars: Racer. Plop into Ani’s plexiglass pod, place your hands on the throttles and pray the Force is with you. All that’s missing is the plasma coupler.
The well-received console game was followed in 2002 by a more aggro sequel, Racer Revenge . With an emphasis on interpod violence, it’s a more fleshed-out game mechanically that never quite took off, a possible casualty of the Prequel backlash.
Criticism was calcifying into consensus and fans had fallen out of love with the pastime of podracing. It would take two decades for another game to pick up the torch, first with the VR title Beyond Victory , followed by Galactic Racer, which proudly features the sport and its foremost ambassadors among several modes of roguelike run-based racing.
Pods aren’t the only way to burn rubber in the Star Wars galaxy. You’ve got ships, speeders, swoops, and, in 2001, super-deformed mascots.
Super Bombad Racing is the first and thus far only Star Wars kart racer. The physics are floaty and fun, and the chibified characters are cute. It won’t unseat Mario, Sonic, or Garfield as kings of kart canon, but it’s unique and almost charming at times, which is more than you can say for a lot of the games we’ve talked about so far.
Thank the maker for the weird ones.
With its jaw-dropping Dinotopia aesthetics and dialogue no sentient being would ever speak, the Prequel Trilogy is George Lucas’s own Death Stranding: the brazen self-belief of an artist with a budget and no one around to say no. Star Wars has been pretty buttoned-up as a brand ever since the Holiday Special, and with Disney at the reins we’re unlikely to see anything as wild as Episodes I, II, and III again.
The games they inspired looked and sounded the part, but rarely matched the unfiltered ingenuity of the films. There are a lot of platformers and third-person action adventures on this list, and even awesome racers and dogfight sims are pretty par for the Star Wars course, but a few titles tried something different.
Lucas founded LucasLearning in 1996, riding the CD-ROM edutainment wave that brought Number Munchers and Incredible Machines to middle school computer labs around the world.
The imprint released several Star Wars Prequel games designed to fit in school curricula, betting on the children’s love of Jar Jar Binks to teach them about fractions and natural science.
Star Wars: The Gungan Frontier sees the titular species in crisis: their bubble cities are overpopulated, they’re surrounded by giant sea monsters, and half the planet can’t stand them.
Boss Nass enlists your aid in colonizing the moon, manipulating its barren ecosystem for imported Naboo flora and fauna in a simplified Sim Life with hints of Spore. Planting trees and balancing the food chain while vibing to the ambient soundtrack is such a pastoral, zen experience that you almost forget that you’re assisting an invasive, extremely annoying species.
Anakin’s Speedway offers kids ages four and up the opportunity to help the enslaved child build tracks for racers to die on, while Pit Droids makes use of the adorable automatons as Lemmings-style problem-solvers, guiding them through mechanical puzzles that teach basic logic and spatial reasoning skills.
The quirky little cluster of learning games are a breath of fresh air after traversing Theed for the thirtieth time, but they didn’t exactly revolutionize early childhood education. If you’re curious how the whole edutainment venture panned out, the last game LucasLearning developed was Super Bombad Racing, which most would agree has little pedagogical value to speak of. The division folded in 2001, ceding the market shortly before the entire space imploded amid widespread internet adoption.
Games have always been quick to chase trends, even the ones based on movies that bucked them at the expense of good taste and narrative coherence. Flash games were in their heyday in the 2000s, and Star Wars embraced the Macromedia madness of it all with a clutch of Prequel-era games for Cartoon Network. More impressive was the expansive browser-based MMO called Clone Wars Adventures that boasted 10 million registered players before it folded in 2014.
Nothing chased a trend harder than Kinect, the much-maligned Microsoft peripheral that jumped on the motion control bandwagon by tracking your body movement with a creepy camera. Kinect Star Wars on the Xbox 360 might be its most infamous title.
The 2012 release is built on the Prequel Trilogy, at least as much as a grab bag of gimmicky minigames can be built on anything. There’s an obligatory podracing mode where you grip a pair of throttles that don’t exist, while the story campaign thrusts you into war as a Padawan of your own design, using the Kinect to control a lightsaber with flailing limbs in a quite uncivilized fashion.
The lasting legacy of Star Wars Kinect, however, has little to do with the Prequels. The Galactic Dance Off is a Just Dance-inspired collection of Now That’s What I Call Music hits repurposed for Star Wars, with parody lyrics that make one yearn for the subtle wit of “Weird Al” Yankovic.
Hollaback Girl becomes Hologram Girl, La Roux’s Bulletproof is Blasterproof, and Jason Derulo's triumphant ode to self-reliance is repurposed as “Han Solo,” spun by DJ Lobot while the titular rogue leads his dance crew of fascist collaborators in moves like “the Trash Compactor.” Even in the weirdest and most embarrassing Prequel game, the Original Trilogy still takes precedence.
LucasArts went down dancing. Kinect Star Wars would be the last game from the legendary studio before Disney moved development out of house, an ignominious end to an uneven era for Star Wars games.
Most of what we’ve discussed so far has been bad to mid at best, with a few standouts brushing against the ceiling of “pretty good.” We wish that we could just wish away our feelings, but it's true: for whatever reason, it’s hard to mine genuine excellence from the Prequel setting. Only a few games have.
Half the video game industry is built by gruff sci-fi people in faceless helmets. Master Chief, Doom Guy, Samus, and more all excel as blank slates on which the player can project. And what slate is blankier than a disposable clone?
In Star Wars: Republic Commando , released in 2005 for the PC and Xbox and set between episodes II and III, you are Boss, the gruff Clone commander of Delta Squad. Despite their genetically identical nature, his subordinates Fixer, Scorch, and Sev have fully-realized personalities all their own, like color-coded Kaminoan Ninja Turtles who obey every order from your contextual squad command button.
Your comrades are so well-written throughout the gritty, violent story that you forget they’re artificial drones at all, and you stop questioning why they have different voice actors despite their larynxes coming from the same vat. The team earned a devoted fan following, their own action figures and spin-off novels, and were clearly homaged by Dave Filoni’s Bad Batch in the Clone Wars cartoon.
Republic Commando’s first-person combat, with an always-appreciated diegetic helmet HUD, gives an infantry grunt’s perspective on the cosmic clash. It’s a more gory affair than typical Star Wars, and that’s saying something for a franchise with so many routine dismemberments. It eschews the esoteric mysticism of the Sith and Jedi and explores the unsung heroes whose blood oils the gears of galactic war like Andor would 17 years later.
Despite being one of the best Star Wars games period, let alone from the Prequel era, Republic Commando never earned a sequel, which means we may never learn the fate of the Clone we left behind. It’s rarely a good idea to get attached to characters when there’s a war on, especially if you’re playing Zero Company .

The UK release of The Phantom Menace was celebrated by revealing the Naboo Starfighter that was hidden in the code. A gleaming art deco Buck Rogers ship that mogged the busted-up Y-wings in the Rebel hangar, the Starfighter made it clear that the future was here, and it was all about the past.

Battle for Naboo is Rogue Squadron with a Prequel coat of paint. Like its predecessor, it’s a mission-based series of skirmishes that makes the most of the N64 Expansion Pak, with a propulsive plot powered by dialogue and dogfights.

The Starfighter itself is back, with a little less aura now that we’ve seen a nine-year-old boy master it in seconds, along with a fleet of the finest ships the Royal Security Forces have to offer. Unlike other games in the series, you play as RSF Lieutenant Gavyn Sykes throughout the whole story. Cool guy, but he’s no Wedge Antilles.

Battle for Naboo is exactly what you’d expect from Rogue Squadron: the Episode I version. The game is most notable for including concept art and an hour of developer’s audio commentary crammed into the N64 cartridge. It was especially impressive in 2001, when DVDs spoiled us with treats and bonus features. We at IGN were sure it was going to be the beginning of a major development trend to come. You can’t always get it right for 30 years.
Factor 5 took their talents back to the OT for the GameCube’s twin Rogue Squadrons, but LucasArts didn’t leave the Prequel age behind.

2001’s Starfighter , the series PS2 debut, is no slouch. Less Star Fox than Ace Combat, the game mixes sim and arcade as it weaves through the narrative of Episode I from the perspective of three characters, including fan favorite Nym, a mononomic space pirate who would one day earn an 18,000 word Wookiepedia article.

Nym and his signature ship, Havoc, would return the next year in Jedi Starfighter , scrapping with Separatists in the antebellum of the Clone Wars. It’s a fuller package than its predecessor, but both rate highly among Prequel games.
For all its faults, the Prequel Trilogy always excelled when it came to space and aerial action, full of big battles between cool looking ships that sound awesome. Now this is podracing!

Actually, this is podracing: Thanks to George Lucas’s lifelong fascination with fast cars, so much of Star Wars is propelled by the energy of a showstopping death race, a promise fully realized in the Phantom Menace.

The film’s entire second act revolves around the Boonta Eve Classic, a 500 mile-an-hour grand prix through the twisted canyons of Tatooine. For the competitors, ILM dreamed up enough pilots to fill a Glup Shitto graveyard, most of whom die horribly while Greg Proops cracks wise. Star Wars: Episode I Racer dares to ask: What’s their story?
The 1999 game for N64 and PC features 23 playable pods, nearly all doomed to expire on Boonta Eve.

We embody racer Ratts Tyerell, family man, racking up wins and wupiupi in the months before he’s vaporized. We become Ben Quadinaros as he purchases pit droids and upgrades his extremely dangerous ride so it doesn’t fail when he needs it most. We are Anakin, forced against our will to endure Watto’s gurgling as we dream of freedom on the track.
